name: The Dominion Mandate and Christian Vocation

objectives.text: Identify that God made people to work and that work is a good gift from him
Name the things God made during the days of creation and recall that he rested from his work
Identify ways Adam was asked to care for the garden and name the animals
Recall that God made people in his image and gave them the job of ruling over and caring for the earth and its creatures
Describe how people in different jobs in a community serve and help their neighbors
Summarize the command in Genesis 1 to be fruitful, fill the earth, subdue it, and have dominion
Explain from Proverbs why diligence in work is wise and laziness is foolish and sinful
Explain the meaning of vocation as God's calling to serve him and others in every area of life
Describe how the curse in Genesis 3 brought toil and frustration into work without making work itself evil
Explain how the pattern of six days of work and one day of rest is grounded in God's own work in creation
Compare working to please people or only to earn pay with working heartily as for the Lord
Distinguish faithful dominion that tends and keeps creation from domination that exploits it
Explain the biblical reasons Christians are called to work, including providing for themselves, serving neighbors, and sharing with those in need
Analyze how human work has value as a reflection of the image of a working God apart from what it earns
Interpret 1 Corinthians 10:31 in its context and apply it to ordinary tasks of school, home, and work
Explain how God equipped Bezalel and Oholiab for skilled work and apply this example to how gifts relate to a calling
Explain how redemption in Christ renews the purpose of work so that labor done in the Lord is not in vain
Explain how Jeremiah's letter instructed exiled Israel to seek the welfare of the city through ordinary work and apply its principle to Christians today
Analyze Tolkien's concept of sub-creation as an account of human creativity flowing from bearing God's image
Construct a theology of work that traces its place in creation, fall, redemption, and consummation
Evaluate the sacred and secular divide in light of the Reformation teaching that every lawful calling can serve God
Defend the dignity of all honest labor using the examples of Jesus the carpenter and Paul the tentmaker
Compare the Reformed understanding of the cultural mandate with other historic Christian views of the relationship between Christ and culture
Evaluate how the cultural mandate and the Great Commission relate as Christians engage culture through their vocations
Create a reasoned account of how a chosen field of work can carry out the dominion mandate and serve neighbors

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (work as good, God as Worker, care of earth, summary of Genesis 1:28, vocation, motives for work, laziness, intrinsic value, 1 Corinthians 10:31, sub-creation, theology of work, sacred and secular divide, dignity of labor, cultural engagement). Dropped the vague 'observe people helping' in favor of a describable objective on neighbor service. Reframed 'connect skills and talents' around Bezalel and calling to avoid the talent stewardship sibling, and reframed 'money vs God' as motives to avoid the economics sibling. Added objectives on the image of God and dominion, the curse on work, the work and rest pattern, dominion versus exploitation, reasons for working, redemption of work, Jeremiah 29, Christ and culture views, the Great Commission relationship, and a capstone vocational account. Added confessional anchors from the Westminster Standards and Heidelberg Catechism where they state the doctrine.
